stages.name: Government intervention: maximum prices
stages.title: Maximum prices
stages.sub: What happens to a market, and to consumers, when the government caps the price below equilibrium.

steps.q: The government caps rent below the price landlords and tenants had settled on in the equilibrium diagram. At that lower price, do more or fewer tenants want to rent than at equilibrium, and do landlords want to offer more or fewer flats?
steps.right: More tenants want flats, but landlords offer fewer
steps.wrong: Fewer tenants want flats, and landlords offer more
steps.hint: A lower price makes buying more attractive but makes selling less attractive.

steps.q: With more tenants wanting flats than landlords are willing to offer at that capped rent, is there enough housing to go round?
steps.right: No, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
steps.wrong: Yes, the market still clears exactly
steps.hint: Look at the gap between the demand and supply curves at the capped price.

steps.q: Compare the capped rent to the old equilibrium rent. For a tenant who does manage to get a flat, is it now cheaper or more expensive than before?
steps.hint: The cap sits below the old equilibrium price.

steps.q: There are not enough flats for everyone who wants one at the capped rent, and price can no longer sort out who gets one. What has to decide who gets a flat instead?
steps.right: Some method other than price, such as queuing or landlord choice
steps.wrong: The price will still sort it out on its own
steps.hint: You know that price normally rations scarce goods between buyers. If price is fixed, what takes over that job?

steps.q: Some tenants missing out on capped flats are desperate enough to pay landlords extra, unofficially, above the legal rent. Does the shortage create a temptation for this kind of illegal deal?
steps.right: Yes, some will trade illegally above the cap
steps.wrong: No, nobody would break the price cap

steps.q: Landlords are now forced to charge a lower rent than before but still face the same costs. To protect their profit margins, what might they do to the flats they offer?
steps.right: Reduce the quality, such as fewer repairs
steps.wrong: Improve the quality to attract more tenants
